utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Madam Registrar, good afternoon. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Start making sure first that all the accused are here, and secondly, that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand. Mr. Popovic, good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in your own language or a language you can understand, please? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Mr. Beara, good afternoon to you too. The same question: I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your own language. THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] I can hear it and understand it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Beara. You may sit down. Mr. Drago Nikolic, good afternoon to you. Same question: Are you receiving interpretation in your own language? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. You may sit down. Mr. Borovcanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear it well and I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. Mr. Miletic, good afternoon to you. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in your own language or a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it and understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Mr. Gvero, good afternoon. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm following the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, you may sit down. And finally, Mr. Pandurevic. Good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language? THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, you may sit down. As on previous occasions, I'd just like to point out to you that if throughout the sitting, the hearing, at any time you're not receiving interpretation clearly, please draw our attention straight away so that we will look into the matter and rectify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go to appearances. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Peter McCloskey for the Prosecution, together with Janet Stewart, our case manager, and attorneys Julian Nicholls and Lada Soljan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey, and good afternoon to you and your team. Appearances for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Zoran Zivanovic for Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Christopher Meek and Nebojsa Mrkic for Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Good afternoon to you. Mr. Beara, for your information, your lead counsel, Mr. Ostojic, sent a letter to the Senior Legal Officer on July -- it says July 29th, 2006; he's living in the future. A few days ago, anyway, he sent a letter to Mr. Von Hebel stating that he will be unable to attend today, that he was delegating Mr. Meek to appear for you. The reason is that his father passed away six months ago in January 18, 2006, and this week, precisely in two days' time, his family will be holding the traditional six-month memorial service, so he asked to be excused. That's the reason why he's not here with us today. Appearances for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Jelena Nikolic and Eleonora Meli Messineo for Mr. Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Stephane Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stephane Bourgon is absent this week. He'll be joining us next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, welcome, and good afternoon to you too. Appearances for Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Counsel Aleksandar Lazarevic appearing for Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, and good afternoon to you. There is ample space where you are sitting. If you can sit somewhere where we can see you, I think we would prefer it. Appearances for Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Natacha Fauveau-Ivanovic, counsel for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic, and welcome. Appearances for Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Defence counsel for Milan Gvero. Together with me is my assistant, Natalie Wagner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you and your team. And finally, appearances for Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. We have a full complement here: Myself and Mr. Sarapa appear for Vinko Pandurevic and we're assisted by our case manager Helena Kaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes, and good afternoon to you and your team. So let me start with two very important developments. First, you see that the Status Conference is being presided over by the three of us today. That's because we have had Judge Prost appointed in time to be here for this Status Conference and, due to the proximity of the commencement of the trial, we thought it best to be all here for the Status Conference. So my first act today is to welcome Judge Prost. This will be the Trial Chamber. The other piece of good news that I am pleased to be able to convey to you is that today I've had confirmation that the Reserve Judge that we will have on this trial has been appointed. He will be here to be sworn in on the 13th of this month in the morning, in time for the Pre-Trial Conference. He is the Norwegian Judge Bjorn Stole, and I will have an opportunity to welcome him as well. I'll go first to the usual formality of trying to remind everyone what everyone knows already, namely the purpose of or reasons for Status Conferences. Last Status Conference was convened by myself on the 19th of May. In light of the proximity, as I said, of the -- of the commencement of the trial, I conferred with the other two Judges, and we came to the conclusion to convene this Status Conference well within the 120-day time limit which is envisaged under the Rules, particularly precisely Rule 65 bis. The purpose of the Status Conference pursuant to the said Rule is to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for the trial. We are almost there, and I hope that this Status Conference will get us there. Secondly, to give an opportunity to the accused to raise issues in relation to their mental and physical conditions as well as other issues they wish to raise. Last time we met we had another accused, Milorad Trbic. For your information, in case you have not been following the developments, is a few days ago, precisely on the 26th of last month, of June, we handed down a decision on severance of Mr. Trbic's case from that of the rest of you. The reasons, succinctly put, are the following: First, we have already set a date for the start of the trial, but there are some pending motions relating to Mr. Trbic, chief amongst which is the Prosecution motion for the referral of his case to Bosnia pursuant to Rule 11 bis, and then there are several outstanding issues related to his health. There is no possibility that any of these decisions be reached or taken before the start of the -- of the trial as planned, so when we decided to sever his case from yours so that your case can proceed without having to wait for the outcome of the Trbic motions. While we are at this, perhaps I can raise a somehow related issue regarding Tolimir. We are about to start the trial, Mr. McCloskey, and Mr. Tolimir still appears in this indictment. We would like to know what are your plans in this regard. In other words, whether what you are -- or what are you contemplating on the matter, whether you intend to ask for Mr. Tolimir's case to be severed from the case that we will be starting in relation to the other accused? Of course, it's your decision, but we need to know because, I mean, there is no point in proceeding with a case with one person still on the indictment if he is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just given that -- what we all know would be the time and expense of -- of trying this case again, we'd like to put that decision off until as long as possible, though the fact that he's on a piece of paper of an indictment doesn't mean we can't just go forward with him on the piece of paper. He's obviously not going forward with us. But if the Court would like us to remove him at some point, I would like to take it perhaps through the -- through the summer recess, and if he's not here after the summer recess, we -- if you wish, we can take him off, though I have no objection to leaving him on. The fact that he's on this indictment doesn't -- doesn't change anything. In fact, it gives everyone the appropriate context factually of having him there. I know some Judges have liked to remove a person, but it's just a piece of paper, and it's a charging document. It doesn't mean anything by itself, as you know. So we can take him off if he's not here after the -- after the summer recess. And the same with Mr. Trbic. I know that there's been some issues about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Trbic has already been severed. There is a motion for reconsideration which we need to consider, and we will decide it in due course, but this is something different. So I do appreciate that you may not have had sufficient time or -- to consult with your superiors on this or that we may be taking you by surprise, but what I suggest is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you can imagine, we discussed this in Chambers before we came here, and our position I wish to reiterate now because we really are in complete disagreement with you when you consider his permanence in the indictment as basically meaning nothing except that his name appears on a piece of paper. We don't want to give the impression that he is being tried in this trial, so we are instructing you to proceed with a motion to have him -- his case severed from that of the others, unless of course you are anticipating producing him within a relatively short time, in other words, before we start. But we wouldn't like to start the trial with Mr. Tolimir still featuring on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I believe Serbia knows where Mr. Tolimir is. I believe Serbia knows where General Mladic is, and if they were of the mood to bring him in, or both of them, they could be here. So hope springs eternal on that, but we will obviously follow your -- your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's start with the first real item on the agenda, first material, significant one. That's outstanding motions. I'll briefly recapitulate what needs to be stated and then follow up from there. You're all aware that the Prosecution way back in -- on 14th June, in the wake of our 31st May decision, followed up with the filing of a Second Consolidated Amended Indictment. Subsequent to that, we have received a number of motions challenging the Second Consolidated Indictment. These were filed on the 23rd and on the 30th of June. I will be coming to these very shortly. The Prosecution sought to file a consolidated response, which has been filed and which we have gone through. We had the intention to -- to issue our decision, to come with our decision on these motions possibly before today, before this Status Conference. That was our desideratum, but there are several issues involved which have engaged us in discussions, particularly Judge Prost appeared on the scene only a few days ago. She was sworn in on the 3rd of July, and therefore it has not been possible for us to have these decisions ready. We are expecting to be -- to come down with -- with our decisions mid next week, in time before the Pre-Trial Conference. Now, you will recall that at the last Status Conference and the previous one we had the issue of some of you not yet having entered a plea, and I'm referring to Mr. Gvero, Mr. Miletic, for the simple reason that they were not in The Hague, they were on provisional release, and Mr. Borovcanin, because of his position in relation to count -- count 2, which we dealt with in our decision of the 31st of May. Now, the various motions that have been filed following the Prosecution filing of the Second Amended Indictment raise the question as to whether there are new charges. Basically, the substance of some of the changes incorporated in the Second Amended Indictment have been questioned by some of you. We have carefully considered both your motions - and I'll be referring to them - both your motions and the situation as it is, and unless Mr. Gvero, Mr. Miletic, and Mr. Borovcanin wish to enter a plea today, then our idea is to postpone the entering of the plea of the part -- on the part of these three accused until Thursday when we have the Pre-Trial Conference. I wish -- I would like to hear feedback from Madam Fauveau, from Mr. Lazarevic, and from you. Would you agree with this or do you prefer to enter a plea today? Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have anything against it. The only thing I remember is that the Consolidated Amended Indictment does not include any new charges against Mr. Miletic. In other words, he already pleaded for all these charges last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite agree with you because the amended indictment changes -- changes a few things for practically every single one of you. But what I want to know is whether you agree to have your client enter pleas next week, or whether he wishes to enter a plea today. To us he hasn't entered any pleas as yet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to consult with my client on that matter. May I go and confer with him for about 20 seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have the same permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lazarevic, your position is a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, my position is actually a very simple one. I believe it's much more practical for my client to enter a plea next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Because we will be dealing with one of the issues that has been raised. Yes, Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my client would like to enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my client would also like to enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will be receiving the pleas from your respective clients later on during this Status Conference while Mr. Borovcanin -- Mr. Borovcanin will enter his pleas this coming Thursday. Thank you. Now, in the previous Status Conferences we had dealt with the way to proceed in relation to two very important motions of the Prosecution, namely the one relating to judicial notice of adjudicated facts and the other one relating to 92 bis statements. We're agreed that you would have 30 days from the -- our decision on Rule 72, on the Rule 72 motions for your responses. I'm very happy to note that you have all respected the deadline. We have received responses from all of you except for Accused Beara. We do not have any responses to these two motions from your lawyers. I just wanted to make that clear. Now, start -- I'll start with the first one. All I need to tell you is that we are studying the -- the responses as well. We had seen already the motion, Prosecution motion. We should be in a position to hand down our decision soon. Still, this will engage us for some time, and we do not consider it as a sine qua non to have it decided before we start the trial, but we will hand down the decision as early as possible. In relation to the Rule 92 bis statement motion, we are waiting for the Prosecution reply, which is due tomorrow, and then we will proceed with dealing -- dealing with it and ultimately deciding, decide it. However, having already studied thoroughly most of the material that accompanied the Prosecution motion, and also having gone through your responses, we would like to raise some issues which are, however, not raised by the Defence. We are raising these issues ourselves. They shouldn't involve you in major problems, but I think you will need to look into some issues. During the prior testimony of quite a number of proposed 92 bis (D) witnesses, Mr. McCloskey, exhibits were used that were admitted in that trial, or in the respective trials, through the testimony of a different witness. These were, for example, maps and photos that were not introduced as part of the witness's testimony but indirectly as they had already been introduced through other witnesses. We haven't got an opportunity to look into these documents for a very simple reason, that upon checking the CD-ROM that you provided, these are not included. It's obvious that the witnesses are referring to these exhibits, but we don't have them. So what -- our position is that we consider it necessary to have these documents if we are to fully evaluate the prior testimony of the proposed 92 bis (D) witnesses. What we suggest is the following: That you provide us and also the Defence with a list which cross-references these exhibits with the proposed exhibit list attached to your 65 ter submission. Basically our problem is this: That we don't know whether these unincluded exhibits are amongst the exhibits that you intend to tender in this -- in this case, and therefore we need this cross-referencing. If -- we don't know whether you intend to tender them in this case in any case. It's not clear. So if you are intending, it's not clear to us which one, which documents will these be and which number you propose to assign, what number you propose to assign, so we need these details. One other practical solution which may fill in this blank, provided it is accompanied with some kind of explanation, is to provide us with -- and the Defence, of course, with a new CD-ROM which would incorporate these unincluded exhibits. That would make it -- make them available to us, also available to the Defence. Most importantly, we need them in order to be able to weigh properly the arguments that you put -- bring forward for the admission of these statements under Rule -- or Rule 92 bis (D). Yes. Any comments on ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just upon first thought, I believe we would be offering, ideally, every exhibit that is referred to by a witness should be offered into evidence, for obvious reasons, to help you make sense out of that witness. We are -- I'm still getting used to the idea of providing exhibits prior to trial that haven't been discussed, but that's fine. No -- no problem there. And all the -- all those exhibits are available to everyone on the judicial database with a few clicks, and practically as easy as on a CD. And we have explained that before. I don't know how computer savvy all of us are. I'm not the best at it, but I know they're there and it's just a few clicks away, be it CD or be it the judicial database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but make that proposition to the Defence. Please don't make it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't like the judicial database?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying we don't like the judicial database. I don't think we should be expected to fill in the blanks for you. If you submitted these statements for us to take into consideration for the purpose of deciding whether to admit them or not under Rule 92 bis, they should be accompanied with the entire documentation and not with part of it and then ask us to go and check the judicial database. That's not part of our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood. And if the Defence has no objection to us providing these other exhibits that were not entered into by these witnesses, that shouldn't be a problem. Having heard no objections, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, let's wait, because the Defence teams, some more than others, take time before they decide whether to answer and what to answer. Are there any comments from any one of you? Yes, Madam Fauveau. I don't know why but I was actually looking at you as if I was expecting you to rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We fully agree with your suggestion. We believe that the Prosecutor should submit all the exhibits produced in the previous trials. However, since these are exhibits that we did not review whilst preparing our response, we'd like to have additional time, maybe not 14 days but additional time to respond with regard to these exhibits. I would also like to add, and I'd like to apologise in advance to the Prosecutor if I'm mistaken, but it seems to me that for some of the proposed witnesses, some of the proposed 92 bis witnesses we have not received all the statements of these witnesses in previous trials. If we moved for a few minutes into private session I could give you the names of the relevant witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to bring that up myself later on, but let's -- let's deal with it now while we're at it. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The thing is this: I don't wish to have this escalate into a matter of controversy, either between the parties or the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. We're making our position very clear: That we are called upon to decide on the proposed admission of over 40 Rule 92 bis statements. It's a laborious exercise. It's an exercise that we do with the utmost attention, and apart from issues relating to whether there should or shouldn't be cross-examination, there is in the initial most fundamental issue involved in each case whether the various requirements under the Rule which would make it possible or make it impossible to admit statements under Rule 92 bis exist or not. For that we need the entire documentation. Some of it is missing. You have been extremely practical in your approach throughout, and I would take it that you will look into this matter and fill in those blanks for us at your earliest, and we -- that would put us in a position to dispose of the motion and the responses within -- within a good time. We've worked a lot already on -- on these issues. As regards what you said, Madam Fauveau, I don't think it's the case of obtaining another 14 days. I mean, once these are disclosed, if there are any other comments or remarks that you would like to add in addition to what you have already submitted in your earlier responses, you are authorised to do that provided we have not decided the Prosecution motion in the meantime. It's not a question of asking for 14 days. That would be provoking unnecessary responses maybe. Is it clear, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your cooperation. I didn't doubt in the least that I would -- that we would find it. Something which is related. It's not exactly Rule 92, it's 94 bis. You had stated earlier on during the 65 ter submissions that you would be filing expert reports pursuant to Rule 94 bis (A), or -- of five of the six experts whose prior testimony you propose for admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis. This is why it is related. What is the position now? How early can we expect you to file the expert reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get right on that along with the exhibits so that you can look at them, hopefully, in the same time frame, because they're so related, as you say. We just, I think, got slightly sidetracked from 92 and 94 and we need to get them more joined together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That's why I said they are related because they are intimately related, but I'm dealing with them separately. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So always in the context of outstanding motions there are two further issues that I will deal with very briefly and then one major issue which will -- on which we will address you and give you instructions, Mr. McCloskey. Now, on the 18th May, the Prosecution filed a motion for protective measures to be extended to five witnesses. We have received the responses -- responses from the Defence teams on the 1st and 2nd June respectively. We are dealing with this, with this motion, and we will decide it in due course. There is also -- or there are two outstanding motions, one by Mr. Miletic, one by Mr. Gvero, requesting temporary provisional release from the 15th of July until the continuation of trial which is anticipated for 14th -- 14th of August. On the 9th of June, the Prosecution filed a response taking no position on this Defence request. We will decide the matter definitively on Thursday when we have the Pre-Trial Conference, or on Friday. So we'll know exactly what your position will be. And this brings me to a very important matter that arises in the wake of the filing of the Second Amended Indictment and the responses that we have received challenging that indictment once more. So I'm referring to a motion filed by you, Mr. Popovic, through your counsel, of course, Mr. Pandurevic, and Mr. Borovcanin, to which the Prosecution filed a consolidated response on the 3rd of July. In addition, Mr. Lazarevic for Mr. Borovcanin filed a -- a reply -- actually, sought permission to file a reply, which he filed in any case. So we have been actively involved in these issues, particularly because there are submissions on the part of defendants in these three motions alleging that there are new charges, new facts, and whatever. As I said earlier, we expect to hand down the decision before the Pre-Trial Conference next week, and we have been actively working on it. However, in anticipation of that decision and for the purpose of it, we are handing down an oral decision now, which is basically the following: Under Article 19 of the Statute and Rule 50 of the Rules, which incidentally also makes cross-reference to Article 19 of the Statute, so under these -- this Article and under this Rule as interpreted in our -- in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Prosecution must provide supporting documentation for every material -- "material proposed amendment to an indictment or it must identify such documentation from the items already in the Trial Chamber's possession to enable the Trial Chamber to determine whether the Prosecution has established a prima facie case with respect to those particular amendments. "The Trial Chamber is of the view that this principle applies equally where an amendment has been proposed on the initiative of the Prosecution as well as when an amendment is made in response to an order of the Trial Chamber. It is our consideration that in response of our decision of the 31st of May, 2006, the Office of the Prosecutor has made a number of material proposed amendments which now appear -- feature in the Second Consolidated Amended Indictment. However, it's also our consideration that the Prosecution has not yet provided the Trial Chamber with the corresponding supporting documentation or, if the documentation is already in the material submitted with the earlier indictment, the Prosecution has not yet identified where in that material the supporting documentation for each proposed amendment can be found. So our disposition is as follows: We are accordingly ordering the Prosecution to provide the Chamber, no later than this coming Monday, the 10th of July, 2006, with supporting documentation or to identify clearly on which pages of the supporting material for the previous indictment such documentation can be found for the following items which are included in the Second Consolidated Amended Indictment. First, paragraph -- when I say "paragraph," these are paragraphs in the decision. Paragraph 30 -- Consolidated Indictment 30.3.1 concerning Nova Kasaba; paragraph 30.4.1 concerning Sandici Meadow; paragraph 30.8.1 concerning Rocevic school; paragraph 30.15.1 concerning Snagovo; and lastly, paragraph 52, alleging that the Bratunac Brigade deliberately targeted civilian areas of the Srebrenica enclave with artillery fire on 25th May, 1995. These are the only five instances where we still need to find out whether there is existing supporting material, short of which you need to provide it. All right? And we are fully confident that you can easily do this by Monday the 10th, which would make it possible for us to hand down our decision then before the Pre-Trial Conference. That's all I had to say in relation to outstanding motions. If there are any matters that you would like to raise only on this subject matter, please go ahead. I see -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, we -- as you mentioned, we have an outstanding application for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. As I'm sure you're aware, there's been a recent Trial Court judgement related to Srebrenica, some slight crossover. We're in the process of reviewing that to see if it is relevant as a citation. As you're aware, having authored that judgement, we are in the process of reviewing that to see if it has relevance. I don't know what you feel about that or if you -- one way or another, but as you can see that the -- our indictment does talk a little bit about that period and there's some -- there's some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't discussed this with my colleagues, obviously, and therefore don't expect me to tell you anything. I do, however, point out to you that I made it very clear in that judgement that the events of 1995 were not an issue in any -- in any manner and whatever was dealt with as historical events are events that have practically been dealt with by every judgement that has been pronounced by this Tribunal dealing with the events in Bosnia. So I think -- I wouldn't like to -- to say more until I have discussed the matter with my two colleagues, and only if the matter is addressed ad hoc by either of you, by the parties. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I also meant to mention the case that came out of Rwanda recently of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's another issue related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a legal issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That we're also reviewing that to see whether it's worth opening this door up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's definitely important for the issue of adjudicated facts, yes, and I think if Defence counsel have not had the opportunity, like it seems you, to address the legal principles enunciated in that decision in relation to genocide, for example, in Rwanda, and you will require an opportunity to address that issue, you will be given opportunity, of course. It applies equally to you and to Defence. I think it's important. Yes. We'll now move on to disclosure matters. Let's start with Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. I anticipate to have a confirmation from you, Mr. McCloskey, that this category of disclosure has been completed by now. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I certainly think so. Let me just -- we believe so. It mentions 92 bis in here as well, so we're working on that. Yes. We have made all efforts. There may be some translations out, although I think we've gotten -- there's just very few translations of some of these witness statements, usually into B/C/S, but we were able to knock off the -- most of them. I don't have the exact number, but we're very -- we were able to work with some Defence counsel and prioritise statements that they were interested in, and I think we've just about -- just about got the translation issues sorted out. As you know, there always seems to be statements hiding somewhere and we're endeavouring to ferret out all of those statements. That's a principal priority here, and we feel pretty comfortable at this point but we'll be continuing to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Of course first I would like to hear any comments that either any of the Defence teams would like to make before I then remind you of what we discussed and we agreed upon at the last Status Conference in relation to 34 witnesses. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with what my learned friend has just said, however, I do have to point out one thing. We still don't have a total of 16 translations, 16 different statements of different kinds of witnesses, and this is something that our clients are not yet familiar with. The list that has been prioritised, and we have received some of these on a CD, but there are some missing. We are talking about another set of statements that have been disclosed to the Defence, statements by various kinds of witnesses from the army and the Ministry of the Interior. The statements are from the Sarajevo trial, statements made to the police or the investigating judge of the Bosnian court, but we don't have a single statement or an interview that the OTP have conducted with these witnesses, and we assume that they must have since these are witnesses who are on their list. There's another witness that the Defence teams so far have been completely unable to identify. This is a member of an OTP team. They conducted the Kravica investigation and a number of interviews related to that investigation. We're not familiar with the substance of that statement. I do not believe this witness has been identified yet, and we certainly don't know who he is. So much for the OTP pre-trial brief, the exhibits, and witness statements as it relates to the list. Disclosure, however, is ongoing, and this has to do with the new archives being opened up in Bosnia and the Republika Srpska on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Any further remarks from any of the Defence teams? The reason why I mentioned this, Mr. McCloskey, is that during -- at the last Status Conference there were 34 witnesses, to my recollection, whose statements had not yet been translated into B/C/S and made available. Now I hear that the list has come down to 16. What I think is that we had given you three weeks from the Status Conference to complete that exercise. I understand that you may have encountered problems. My preoccupation, and I'm sure it would be the preoccupation of my colleagues, too, is if any of these 16 witnesses whose statements have not yet been provided in B/C/S are amongst the first set of witnesses to be heard until the end of September, because if that is the case, I would enjoin you straight away to accelerate the process and make sure that they are made available before we start the trial. If not, we will give you a further chance, of course, which would reflect also your difficulties, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe the list is closer to five, and it gets smaller every day. So -- and we have good communication with counsel normally, and I don't have any outstanding priority requests or concerns from counsel aside from what I've heard today, and we'll work with them and get right on that, so anything that comes to our doorstep we'll work with, but right now I've got no requests except for what I've just heard, and we're close to that, but we are focusing definitely on that group of first witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. We are not establishing any further deadlines. We are fully trusting you, Mr. McCloskey, that you are dealing with this matter within the limits of what is possible. You will recall during the previous Status Conference we had mentioned the report of the military expert Butler. This was submitted by 9th June. I understand, however, that until a few days ago, until the end of last month, end of June, the Prosecution had not yet received the B/C/S translation of the material. Can I have a confirmation of that from the Defence teams? You have received the report but you have not received the B/C/S version of it? Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the translation arrived today, we haven't received it yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. This is a problem that needs to be addressed and which can be addressed with relative ease because the CD that was made available contains the report in English and there is some material already existing in B/C/S. So I don't see why it has not been made available to the Defence in B/C/S too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The report was submitted to CLSS the day afterward and we have not received it back yet. And they've been doing a very good job at working under tremendous pressure. So we will check with them and get an estimated date for that. The materials Mr. Butler mentions in his report are hyperlinked and are in original B/C/S for that help, but we haven't received it back from CLSS yet, but we hope to soon, but I haven't checked with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the thing is this: How early in the trial do you expect to produce -- to be dealing with this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler would be several months down the road, which is normal because it's more appropriate for everyone to see a lot of material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just wanted to make sure that he will not be amongst the early witnesses to be brought over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this has been discussed somewhat with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the famous hard disk that appeared and disappeared. Let's hope that everyone has seen it and everyone knows where it is. The Rule 68 disclosure. Mr. Haynes, you and Ms. Soljan had the last word. After some big efforts, the hard disk was traced, was found, and that was supposed to make the round --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how comfortable I am being spokesman on this particular topic. The hard disk drive was found to be more usable by being converted into a series of DVDs. We had those burnt and copied and made them available to those who wished to have them. The original hard disk drive is back with the Office of the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. Are you satisfied with -- now, I'm not addressing you as a spokesman, I'm just addressing all the Defence teams: Are you all satisfied with the standard of Rule 68 disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Speaking for my part, I think we still find EDS a better system to search than the hard disk drive. The hard disk drive is, of course, more portable but the searching is not very good. But that's just for my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further remarks from any of the Defence teams? Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's a question which is not at all technical. I'm perfectly aware the Prosecutor has tried to identify the documents for Rule 68 as best he can, but he's not always in a position to identify the documents, exculpatory material. Another problem in this procedure is that today we have seven accused. We received documents for 68, and we don't know immediately which accused is concerned. It's rather difficult. It doesn't really help us, because when we receive 68 documents, if they don't concern this or that accused, for us its documents which are equivalent to others, whether it is 68 or another. We have to analyse it, see it, appreciate, evaluate in the same way. The identification of Rule 68 doesn't mean much in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a position on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau asked -- was one, I think the only, counsel that provided us with a bit of an outline of some of the material she thought was Rule 68, and we endeavoured to provide her with that material, and recently, I believe, an index of that material. So that was the material specifically for her concerns. I believe we gave that everyone as well, naturally. Rule 68 is such a broad, broad, broad topic, especially as it goes to the potential -- for example, a statement that may be in conflict with a witness's statement is Rule 68. So it has not been our intention to go through for seven accused and find out where this person may be consistent or inconsistent. It's an impossible, impossible task. So it's not the Prosecution's position to try to identify individual accused Rule 68. If we find something that is -- actually appears to be exculpatory, we will -- I mean, when I say "appears to be exculpatory," that's different than the broad ambit of Rule 68. We will tell the Defence that. And something that suggests that Mr. Beara wasn't in Bosnia in July of 1995, we would absolutely give them that document, and they would see what it was. We don't have any such document. So anything that rises to the level of exculpatory evidence of that nature, yes, certainly, we would. We'd tell them and identify it to them, but the masses of what could be possibly inconsistent or they may consider to be Rule 68. For example, what Ms. Fauveau asked for I don't personally consider to be Rule 68. A lot of Muslim material. But she asked for it, and she -- and that's what her defence may involve, so we got that for her. But to try -- for me to sort out what I think is Rule 68, I don't think there is any Rule 68 in that, but if it looks substantive, if it looks like some significant piece of material, no problem, we can alert them to that, and -- besides giving them the material. But we don't generally give them great big hunks of, you know, a thousand-page document and say this is Rule 68. It's usually these documents come in one- or two-page forms, or they're an intercept that is one or two pages, and they -- each document speaks for itself. So it's not a difficult process document by document. And there's not -- you know, we're not identifying all that much Rule 68. I mean, we're looking, but we're not -- it's not a massive amount of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I won't say much at this stage, but I get the impression that you have a somewhat distorted idea of what Rule 68(i) is all about and how it has been interpreted throughout the years. In spite of various attempts to have the first paragraph changed, it's still as it is and as it was, which is material which is in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor. I've already decided on more than one occasion that you cannot rely on the electronic database and say everything is available there, therefore, I don't have to go through the material and identify exculpatory material. I agree with you that you shouldn't look at Rule 68 as applying to the collectivity. It should apply to each and every individual accused here. It's your responsibility if you have material which in your knowledge is -- may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused to disclose it. I don't want to pass through the unfortunate experience I had in Oric where, throughout the entire trial, even from -- even before the commencement of the trial, there are allegations of Rule 68 material being available in the hands of the Prosecution and being withheld in violation of Rule 68. And this went right not only through the entire trial but until two days before we handed down the decision. All of a sudden the Prosecution discovered another bulk, bulk, an amount of documents, quite bulky, that went to either suggest not the absence of guilt or -- in that case it was absence of guilt of the accused, and it had not been disclosed. I don't want to find ourselves in that situation because it will require us to take drastic action as we go -- as we go along. It's your responsibility. Whatever changes were effected to Rule 68 in the past years have never affected the obligations that you have under the first paragraph of Rule 68. I won't say more, but if there are any doubts as to whether a particular piece of material is exculpatory or not, the practice has been not for you to decide that it is not but for you or the Defence or for both of you to refer it to the Trial Chamber and then the Trial Chamber will decide whether it is exculpatory or not. If, on the face of it, it is exculpatory, then you have an obligation to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- I want to be perfectly clear: I do not believe just giving them EDS that overrides my Rule 68 obligation. In no way. What I was speaking of is they were suggesting that I need to identify precisely in a document what is Rule 68 and which accused it has to do with. That's what I was objecting to. And I was saying that if I have something that that's obvious I will give it to them and talk to them about it. That's easy. But the vast amount of material that may be Rule 68, that we may provide to them as Rule 68, we will make every effort to identify it and provide it to them and I guarantee you will not go through the experience you went through with Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not. However, what your responsibilities are under Rule 68 are clearly stated in the Rule, and we take it that you will act accordingly. I hope we will not pass through what I passed through in Oric, repeated and flagrant violations of Rule 68, flagrant. So any further submissions in relation to Rule 68 disclosure, and any other kind of disclosure, for that matter, before I close on this part of the agenda? I see none. Let's move to agreed facts. Yes. I see a few smiles on the face -- on some of the faces. Have you endeavoured to try and meet and come forward with some agreed facts? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We a long time back sent quite a few facts and we got a couple of responses with a few facts but not anything that would help the Court or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't it possible for various Defence teams to take a practical approach and agree on what could be agreed upon without compromising the position of your respective clients? Absolute silence. Mr. Lazarevic won't even look at us. Absolute silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have absolutely no problem with looking at you. What I can assure you is that we're not avoiding any such conversation with the Prosecution. We were quite busy in last couple of weeks dealing with all these motions, all these submissions that you're all aware of, and we're just -- we are not avoiding discussion with the Prosecution. Let them file the motion asking for our assistance and we will sit and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to this again Thursday during the Pre-Trial Conference and see whether there have been any positive developments. I'll pretend to be optimistic for once. Let's go into private session now, please. We need to discuss something in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everyone is here. Yes. Before we proceed on the same subject matter, we are in open session, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Krgovic, may I ask you to be kind enough to approach your respective clients for the purpose of entering the plea, whether they will waive the right to have the indictment read out in its entirety as far as they are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We waive this right. It's not necessary to read the whole indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's not necessary to read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to make sure of that because we would have to regulate our schedule accordingly otherwise. Okay. So we have discussed in the meantime about your preferences in relation to (redacted). Let's go into private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back to open session. Mr. McCloskey, I think we have settled now that opening statements of the Prosecution will be made on -- starting on the 21st of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is my understanding. That's what we've been planning on. We would not complain if it was August 28th, and I know the Defence had some issues on that, but we've seen August 21st and understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. As an addition to that, please consult your clients to see what you'll be -- your decision in relation to any opening statements that you may wish to make, you or your clients according to the existing rules. We would appreciate having the relative information from you in good time so that we can plan ahead, especially since, if there are no statements to be expected from Defence, then the Prosecution must be put notice of that so they bring forward the witnesses without any time wasting. Actually we had agreed in the Status Conference of 19 May that today you should be in a position to give us that indication. So if any one of you is in a position to give us an indication now, it would help us immensely to plan ahead. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I shan't be making an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe it's the intention of our Defence team to also make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I said I wouldn't, but I -- the transcript will reveal the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm looking at you. So you intend to make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, at this point I believe that an opening statement will be made, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other indication? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I not make opening statement too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You won't. My previous question also was directed to obtain information whether any of the accused would be making any statements. Of course that is a choice, an option that is available under the Rules. Let's put it like this: Can I ask all of -- each and every one of you to decide on this between now and the Pre-Trial Conference on Tuesday [sic] and come back with an affirmative position on -- on this, definitive position on this. All right. We have that of Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Meek, and Mr. Haynes. And the others, please, will be asked the same question on Thursday when we meet next. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just something about the transcript. The transcript says that the Pre-Trial Conference will be held on Tuesday. I think we're talking about a Thursday, Thursday the 13th, and we believe that this a useful instruction from the Chamber because we do need to confer with our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much for pointing out the transcript error, which I'm sure will be corrected. And of course we do appreciate that you need to consult with your clients on this, but please on Thursday try to give us your position. Now, the work -- the work plan. Let's go through what we have agreed upon, and I want to make sure that the pattern that has been followed very efficiently, I must say, by both of you will continue until we come to the commencement of the trial. I had said earlier on that you have been very punctual in filing all your responses relating to Rule 92 bis motion and the adjudicated facts by the deadline. We established the last time we met that the -- we had to shift somewhat the other dates that we had communicated to you in a way which would find us have the Pre-Trial Conference on Thursday coming, the 13th, then tentatively start with the trial on the 14th with the understanding that there will not be the opening statements on that day. We had also agreed that when -- then we will adjourn until August, and -- both on the 14th, and when we reconvene in August, we will conclude on various initial procedural issues that need to be taken care of, need to be taken care of, amongst which, of course, there will be the question on how we will be regulating the time to be allocated for examination-in-chief and also cross-examination considering that you are now seven -- seven teams. During that stage, we will, I hope, already we would have handed down the decision both on the adjudicated facts and the Rule 92 bis, which would enable the Prosecution to be in a better position to give an indication to the Trial Chamber how long you anticipate your -- your case to last, because I understand that until you have those two decisions in place, you can speculate but you may not necessarily be near the -- the real situation. We had also agreed that because of this shifting, and while initially I had told you you would have until the 14th of July to file your pre-trial Defence briefs, that that was brought forward by two days, and we agreed that that would be advanced to July 12th so that when we start the Pre-Trial Conference the day after, we'll have something in our hand, knowing that we will not be able to conclude in any case. But I want to make sure that you are all preparing to meet this deadline which would help us immensely when we come to the Pre-Trial Conference. I have your commitment. We had agreed also that there will not be the need for the Trial Chamber to issue a Scheduling Order because so far you have kept to your commitments and we have no reason to -- to doubt your word. Yes. So the understanding is that by Wednesday, end of business on Wednesday, you would come forward with your pre-trial Defence briefs in accordance with what is required by -- by the Rules. Then the understanding is that -- what is left over after the 13th will have to be taken up on the 14th or later on in August when we meet again. The proofing chart. Those of you who have been following the developments, know that just for the witnesses' documents that will be made use by the end of September, the Prosecution has provided all this material. And that made us understand a little bit better why they were encountering problems in completing the proofing chart. We understand your problems, and for that reason we have revised a little bit our assessment which we had communicated earlier, and the position is as we have handed it down in our decision. This covers the testimony until the end of September. Then by the 18th of August you need to deal with the rest of the witnesses, and by the 31st of October you need to complete the proofing chart in relation to the documentation, to all the documentation. We trust you will make every effort. We've been cooperative, we've been forthcoming with you, and we expect you to be as cooperative as you have been already. And there's the question of length of trial. There is one defendant, one accused, less now. Mr. Trbic is out of the scene is for the time being for sure. Does that affect your earlier prognosis of the anticipated time required, Mr. McCloskey, or minimally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would say minimally because most of the Trbic witnesses were witnesses that would have been called anyway, and the time that cross-examination would take wouldn't have been that much more with just one more lawyer, so I can't think of any reason why that is a big savings of time, but it's some and every little bit helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I mentioned earlier the question of cross-examination and examination-in-chief. What I suggest on behalf of the Trial Chamber is that between now and when we next meet you try to discuss this amongst yourselves, between yourselves, because it would help immensely the Trial Chamber when it comes to deliberating on -- on the issue. If there is an agreement between you, that is always an advantage. In the meantime, may I also draw your attention to the decision of the Appeals Chamber of a couple of days ago which relates to the decision that had been taken in the Prlic case regarding the distribution of and allocation of time for the purpose of examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. I think it would be very useful to you to have a good look at it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. President, the Prosecution fully supports the decision as it set that out. I think that was an excellent decision, and it gives the Defence also some room to move. So we fully support the basic precepts of that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not ask the Defence today for a position on this. Yes, Mr. Meek? You disagree with that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. On behalf of the accused Beara, we don't think that decision was very good at all, however we do agree with the Prosecution that they should start their opening statements on the 28th of August rather than the 21st. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not have your wishes fulfilled, Mr. Meek. We'll start on the 21st of August with the opening statements. So at the same time and on the same score, if -- we will be coming back to you later on for your submissions in relation to the distribution and allocation of time for the purposes of examination-in-chief and cross-examination. Now, the most solemn part of today's Status Conference, Mr. Miletic and Mr. Gvero, I will be proceeding on behalf of the Trial Chamber to enter a plea to the counts which are applicable to you. Madam Fauveau and Mr. Krgovic, the facts I'm referring to are the counts as they are in the indictment of the 11th November, 2005. Let me make something clear. This is the indictment they would have entered a plea upon had they been present together with the others when pleas of -- were entered. Now, it may well be that as a result of the decision that we plan to hand down in the coming week there will be the need to come back to some or more or all of the accused to re-enter pleas. That's quite possible, but for the time being, I think what we need to concentrate upon are the charges that arise, emerge from the indictment of the 11th November, 2005, and I take it that there is a waiver. We don't need to read the indictment. Can I proceed with Mr. Miletic, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Miletic, please stand up. I am very soon asking you -- going to ask you to tell me whether you wish to enter a plea to the various indictments that concern you and that are brought against you by the so-called Consolidated Amended Indictment of the 11th November, 2005. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have also waived your right to have the indictment in its relevant parts read out to you, but I want to know first and foremost whether you are aware of the contents of this indictment as it relates to you, the various counts that relate to you, and whether you understand the import of the substance of these counts and the accusations that are brought against you. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand. I understand the counts. I understand the indictment in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gvero, I take it therefore that you have read the Consolidated Indictment and that you have also -- not Mr. Gvero, sorry, Mr. Miletic. I apologise to you, Mr. Gvero, you may remain seated. Mr. Miletic, I take it therefore that you have read the Consolidated Amended Indictment that was provided to you in your own language and you've had an opportunity to discuss it with your counsel and take advice from him? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes. Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you prepared to enter your pleas to the various counts that are applicable to you today? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Miletic, that you are charged under count 4, count 5, count 6, count 7, count 8 of the Consolidated Indictment, Amended Indictment. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll start with count 4. Count 4 of the Consolidated Amended Indictment charges you with murder, this being a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(A) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count of murder; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And the registrar will enter into the record that the accused has pleaded not guilty to count 4. We move to count 5. This count charges you with -- again with murder, however this time murder is being charged as a violation of the laws or customs of war punishable under Articles 3, and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this fifth count of murder; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Miletic. We move to count 6, which charges you with persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, this being a crime against humanity, and it includes murder, cruel and inhumane treatment, terrorising the civilian population, destruction of personal property and forcible transfer, punishable under Articles 5(H) and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count 6 of persecutions; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Miletic. We move to count 7 which charges you with inhumane acts consisting in forcible transfer, this being a crime against humanity which is punishable under Articles 5(I) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this seventh count of inhumane acts consisting in forcible transfer; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last count applicable to you is count 8, which charges you with deportation, this being a crime against humanity punishable under Articles 5(D) and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this final count 8 of deportation; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. -- Please, Mr. Gvero, you were disturbing. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were disturbing us. You shouldn't be laughing. You were disturbing us. This is a very -- this is a very solemn moment, Mr. Gvero. You're not understanding the solemnity of this moment when you're asked to enter a plea. Then you better learn it and learn it very quickly. Mr. Miletic was entering a plea and you were talking aloud to your colleague over there. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I was seeking some information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may remain standing for the time being because we're coming to you. Madam Registrar, could you enter into the records that accused Miletic pleaded not guilty to all the counts that were referred to him; counts 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the Consolidated Amended Indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. We come to you, Mr. Gvero. And I start with putting the same questions to you. Have you read the Consolidated Amended Indictment? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was delivered to you, handed to you in your own language? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... language. And have you had an opportunity to discuss it with Mr. Krgovic? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take advice from him? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand what you're being charged with under the counts -- the same counts that I actually read out to Mr. Miletic? Do you understand the import or the substance of these counts and the charges contained therein? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've read the indictment and I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you prepared to enter your plea today? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Indeed I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with count 4, Mr. Gvero, which charges you with murder, a crime against humanity punishable under Articles 5(A) and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count 4, murder, a crime against humanity; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Count 5 charges you with murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Article 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this count 5 of murder being a violation of the laws or customs of war; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And count 6 charges you with persecutions on political, racial, and religious grounds, this being a crime against humanity and which includes murder, cruel and inhumane treatment, terrorising the civilian population, destruction of personal property and forcible transfer punishable under articles 5(H) and 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this sixth count, namely one of persecution? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And count 7 charges with you inhumane acts, being forcible transfer, a crime against humanity, also punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this 7th count of inhumane acts; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And finally count 8, which charges you with deportation, being a crime against humanity punishable under Articles 5(D) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. How do you wish to plead to this eighth count, being one of deportation; guilty or not guilty? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, I wish to apologise once again. It wasn't my intention to disturb. I was just seeking some information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Gvero. And, Madam Registrar, could you kindly enter into the records of case the fact that the accused Gvero has pleaded not guilty to counts 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 of the Consolidated Amended Indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. You may sit down, Mr. Gvero. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we come to the next item, namely -- you know that I've explained it to you in the past that we are required by the Rules each time we have a Status Conference to inquire from you -- of you the state of your detention, any issues you may wish to raise in relation to that state of detention but also in relation to your state of health and other -- any other matter that you would like to raise. I start with you, Mr. Popovic. And before -- before I give you the floor, I wish to inform you that following your address to me as the Pre-Trial Judge in May when we had the last Status Conference, I instructed the Registrar of this Tribunal to inquire for the Trial Chamber -- make a full inquiry following your complaint, and we have had a series of information coming from the Registrar based upon information he was receiving from the Detention Unit. The final outcome is that according to the information contained therein is, yes, it's true, you were diagnosed with diabetes type 2 when you first arrived. Before I continue, last time you told me that you did not have any problem with having this discussed in open session. If you wish to have this discussed in private session, we can go into private session. It's up to you. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] No need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the information that I have, because I also asked for the medical reports that are in your file to see what treatment you have been receiving, indicate that you were first -- you had some analysis carried out, laboratory analysis to establish your condition and also what treatment you required, that you have been under treatment since your arrival. That's an oral administration of some drug. I have the name but I can't remember it. I'm also told that once a month your blood sugar level is tested and that every effort is made to provide you with meals that are adequate for persons who have this diabetes type 2 condition. I wish confirmation -- I would like confirmation from you that the information that I have received is correct, and then of course you are free to make any additional statement that you may wish to. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. "Very well" means what? It is correct? In other words, the information that I have been given is correct? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Correct, yes. Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further concerns which relate to your state of detention and also your state of health that you would like to communicate to the Trial Chamber today? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] For the time being, there's nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate your honesty, Mr. Popovic. Please make yourself comfortable, and let me move to Mr. Beara. The same question to you: If you have got any issues you'd like to raise in relation to both detention and state of health or any other issue, please come forward. THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No. I haven't got anything, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Beara. Mr. Nikolic, same question. Same question to you. THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no objections whatsoever to the conditions in the Detention Unit. My health is good. There are no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Borovcanin -- you may sit down. Mr. Borovcanin. THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing particular to say. Everything is as usual except that two days ago I broke my foot during sport activities, but I have been treated properly and there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please keep us informed if you encounter any problems in this regard. THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] If things get worse, I will let you know, but if they move for the better I assume there's no need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you. Mr. Miletic, I know that you've been here only a couple of days, and hopefully you won't have to stay much longer for the time being, but I would like to know whether you have any concerns in relation to your state of detention and physical or mental health. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as usual, I have no objections. I'm a soldier, and I do not complain. I am satisfied with the conditions here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Miletic. Mr. Gvero -- you may sit down. Mr. Gvero, same question to you: Do you have any concerns in relation -- THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do have some health problems. However, they're not recent ones. They are kept under control, I'm being treated well, and I hope that things will remain that way. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Gvero. Mr. Pandurevic. THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Are there any other matters that either of you would like to raise before we adjourn to Thursday? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of issues going back a bit to discovery that I have everyone here that I want to alert folks to. As they're aware, there's been a trial related to this case in -- in Belgrade, the Skorpion trial. There's an ongoing trial in Sarajevo right now regarding the Kravica case, and there is also now a trial in Boston regarding the trial of a -- Boston, Massachusetts, the trial of a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment related to his conduct in our case. We're endeavouring to find the information and the testimony that will be relevant in this case as there will undoubtedly be Rule 68 in that there will be inconsistencies, however, there's no easy answers to this. In any of those three jurisdictions it's not as simple as just getting a transcript. So we're endeavouring to identify that material and capture it and get it out to everyone as soon as possible, but as you can imagine, given the nature of this case and that there's cases all over the world on it, it's an interesting endeavour to be -- to be involved in. That in combination, I expect to get a report within the next week about the level of material in these Banja Luka archives, just to determine if there is -- seems to be voluminous material so -- that's significant to our case or not. And I don't know anything on that yet, but I should have it soon and I will, of course, be in touch with everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to these other cases that you mention, of course that information may or may not become easily accessible depending on circumstances. You know what happened in the Ovcara trial, how long it took to obtain information. It may not be easy. However, I do appreciate, of course, that you realise your involvement and obligations under the Rules, and we would appreciate, of course, every effort that you put into this. In relation to the Banja Luka archive or documents, these have now been in possession of the Trial Chamber for a year, I would imagine, or just under a year. They were being consulted already during the Prosecution case in Oric, and that finished -- and that finished in -- Prosecution finished in January of -- of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will double-check that, but it's my understanding that this is something that we've become aware of just in the last few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. The Banja Luka collection has been in the possession of the Prosecution -- while the Oric Prosecution case was still ongoing, and I had this special problem with the Prosecution at the time precisely because of Rule 68 disclosure -- disclosure issues. But there was someone already from the Office of the Prosecutor analysing this entire collection at the time.
